summary.title: Writing a minimal x86-64 JIT compiler in C++ - Part 1
summary.one_liner: You learn how to hand-assemble x86-64 machine code into a byte vector in C++, copy it into mmap'd executable memory, and call it as a function at runtime.
keywords: ahead of time vs just in time compilation
bjarne stroustrup a tour of c++
takeaways: JIT compilation means generating machine code at runtime, unlike AOT-compiled C++ which cannot change after compilation.
Machine code is specific to both the processor (x86-64 here) and the operating system, so syscall numbers differ between Linux and macOS.
Assemble a small x86-64 function, disassemble it with objdump to get the exact bytes, and store those bytes in a std::vector of uint8_t.
Allocate pages with mmap in a multiple of the page size, copy the code in, and cast the pointer to a function pointer to call it.
summary.summary: The article is Part 1 of a series on building a minimal x86-64 JIT compiler in C++ that targets Linux and macOS, with WSL as a possible route on Windows. The author builds a simple program that asks for a name and generates a greeting() function at runtime. The workflow is: write the function in x86-64 assembly, assemble and disassemble it with objdump to get the bytes, store those bytes in a vector of uint8_t (with the message length and text patched in), then copy them into mmap-allocated executable memory and call through a function pointer. Code was tested with GCC 5.4 on Linux and Apple Clang 9.0.0 and GCC 7.2 on macOS. Part 2 covers calling a C++ function from generated code.
